title: Permutations & Combinations
description: Counting arrangements and selections, the foundation of combinatorics problems

blocks.text: Permutations and combinations are the core of counting. They answer two questions that appear constantly: in how many ways can we arrange things, and in how many ways can we choose things.
Getting the difference right, and knowing the formulas, is the foundation of every combinatorics problem.
Counting starts with one simple rule. If one choice can be made in A ways and an independent second choice in B ways, then together they can be made in A times B ways.
For example, 3 shirts and 4 trousers give 3 times 4, which is 12 outfits. Almost all counting formulas grow out of this single principle.

A permutation is an arrangement where the order counts. Arranging n distinct items in a row can be done in n factorial ways, since there are n choices for the first spot, n minus 1 for the next, and so on.

blocks.caption: Order matters for permutations, but is ignored for combinations

blocks.text: If you arrange only r of the n items, the count is n factorial divided by (n minus r) factorial, written as nPr.
A combination is a selection where order does not matter. Choosing 2 people from a group is the same set no matter which you name first.

The count, written nCr or C(n, r), is n factorial divided by r factorial times (n minus r) factorial. It equals the permutation count divided by r factorial, because each unordered choice was counted r factorial times as ordered arrangements.

Quick test:

Ask yourself: if I swap the order, is it a different outcome? If yes, it is a permutation. If no, it is a combination.

content.title: 4. Pascal Triangle and the Key Identity

blocks.text: Binomial coefficients follow a beautiful pattern. Each C(n, k) equals the sum of the two values above it, C(n minus 1, k minus 1) plus C(n minus 1, k). This is Pascal identity.

blocks.caption: Pascal identity: each binomial coefficient is the sum of the two above it
blocks.alt: Pascal Triangle and the Key Identity

blocks.text: This gives an easy way to build a table of all binomial coefficients with only additions, which is handy when you need many of them and want to avoid factorials.
For small values, compute nCr with a single loop, multiplying and dividing as you go so the intermediate value stays a whole number.
When answers must be taken modulo a prime, compute factorials modulo that prime and divide using a modular inverse, which relies on fast exponentiation.
Counting arrangements and selections is everywhere.
